summary: Orbi’s Mission Lab is a browser game where kids aged 6 and up, plus older players in Engineer mode, design a complete space mission from start to finish. Players pick a mission goal, a destination and a real rocket with 2026 prices, then build a spacecraft from part cards: body, power, science instruments and radio. Live meters show how every choice changes mass, power, budget, data, communications and risk, so players feel the same trade-offs real engineers face. They then launch, fly key moments themselves with real physics, handle timed emergencies like space junk and solar storms, and get a report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed. Up to 4 players can work as a crew with different roles. The game matters because it turns NASA’s systems-engineering thinking into play any child can understand, in English, Kazakh and Russian, on any phone or computer.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Orbi’s Mission Lab is a browser game where players design and fly a complete space mission. They pick a mission (a first CubeSat, wildfire watch, Aral Sea watch, Moon ice mapping, a telescope at L2, Mars, Jupiter, a custom mission, or a copy of a real NASA mission). They choose an orbit and a real launch vehicle with real 2026 prices and capacities, then build the spacecraft from part cards: body, power, science instruments and radio. Live meters show weight against rocket capacity, electricity, budget, data sent home, radio link, schedule and risk. Before launch, a crew of 1 to 4 players, each with a role and a secret goal, must agree. The mission then runs month by month with real events such as solar storms, space junk and part failures. Players fly the launch and the orbit capture burn themselves and react to timed emergencies. The report gives a score, up to 3 stars, a “Why this result?” explanation and a comparison with real NASA missions. Behind the game, a physics engine models the rocket equation and delta-v, orbits and eclipses, solar power versus distance, batteries, radio link budgets, data volume, radiation, orbit decay, cost and reliability.

Benefits and intended impact:
Children learn that every engineering choice affects everything else, and why real missions look the way they do. The game needs only a web browser, works on phones, tablets and computers, and is available in English, Kazakh and Russian. That makes it easy for teachers to use in class, including in countries with fewer space-education resources. We want young players to see space engineering as something they can understand and someday do.

Creativity:
Players don’t just pick parts and read a score. They fly the critical moments themselves with real physics: a gravity-turn launch, an orbit capture burn where the real Oberth effect rewards good timing, dodging space junk and stopping a tumble. Other creative parts are Pilot School, Career mode (run a space agency and race a rival to Mars and Jupiter), a Real Missions Museum with 20 real spacecraft, a cabin window for taking photos of real places drawn in cartoon style, and Orbi, a robot guide who explains problems in kid language.

Factors we considered:

  • Accuracy: real formulas and real prices, plus real rules, such as NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative launches being open only to US teams.
  • Balance: three stars are possible only when every main goal is met, and Orbi’s fixes cost points.
  • Accessibility: Easy and Engineer modes, big buttons, phone and tablet layouts, and three languages.
  • Clear feedback: every failure explains why it happened and how to fix it.
  • Teamwork: roles, secret goals and a shared “Go” vote.

Tools:
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page with no installation, Canvas graphics, Web Audio for music and sound, and Python scripts for testing and drawing the cartoon planet maps. It is hosted on GitHub Pages and was built with Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant.
